151.quote_or_event: “…steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean, mild like the moon, refulgent like the sun, pure like excellent gold; like the earth he patiently bore everything; like a well-kindled fire he shone in his splendour.”
151.explanation: The Kalpa Sūtra describes Mahāvīra during his years as a wandering ascetic with a string of similes, and patient endurance is given the image of the earth, which bears everything.
151.tie_back: Valluvar opens his chapter on patience with the earth that holds up even those who dig into it, and Jain scripture uses the same image, 'like the earth he patiently bore everything', for Mahāvīra's forbearance.
151.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra § 118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
151._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The earth-as-patience image is a direct parallel, though the Kalpa Sūtra gives it as one simile among many rather than spelling out the 'those who dig into it' point.

152.quote_or_event: “If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
152.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) a Jain monk must bear, abuse is met not only with silence but by refusing to let the words lodge in the mind.
152.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to bear even wrongs that go beyond all limits and, better still, to forget them, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise moves from bearing ('silently overlook') to letting go ('not take them to heart').
152.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
152._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It is a strong fit for 'bear, then forget', though it is addressed to monks and covers abusive words rather than every kind of wrong.

153.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry.”
153.explanation: Jacobi notes that the word translated 'child' (bāla) also means an ignorant man. Mahāvīra's teaching is that one who answers a fool's abuse with anger becomes a fool too, so patience is the stronger course.
153.tie_back: Valluvar calls bearing with fools the greatest strength of all, and the Uttarādhyayana gives the same rule of not raging at the ignorant, though it has no counterpart to the Kural's first half on failing a guest.
153.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
153._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, including Jacobi's note 'Or like an ignorant man, bâla'. It matches only the half of the kural about patience with fools; the hospitality half is not covered.

154.quote_or_event: “Supreme forbearance–uttama kṣamā, supreme modesty–uttama mārdava, supreme straightforwardness–uttama ārjava … constitute ten virtues (dharma).”
154.explanation: The Tattvārthasūtra puts forbearance first among the ten virtues that stop new karma from flowing into the soul. Pūjyapāda glosses it as freedom from anger when meeting 'insolent words, ridicule or derision, disgrace, bodily torment' from vicious people.
154.tie_back: Valluvar says that whoever wants to keep his completeness of character (நிறை) must cherish patience, and in Jainism forbearance comes first among the virtues that keep the soul's purity whole against incoming karma.
154.source: Tattvārthasūtra 9.6, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
154._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (the ellipsis shortens the list). It is a strong thematic fit for patience as the foundation of moral integrity, but the Jain framing of protecting the soul from karmic influx differs from the Kural's ideal of character.

155.quote_or_event: “The young man's self-restraint is self-restraint. The gift of him who owns no stores of wealth is gift indeed. When man has means and might to punish every fault, if he forbear, call him the patient man.”
155.explanation: In its chapter on meekness, the Jain-authored Nālaṭiyār says that real forbearance belongs to the man who has the power to punish and holds back.
155.tie_back: Valluvar contrasts those who punish (ஒறுத்தார்), whom the world counts as nothing, with those who forbear (பொறுத்தார்), whom it treasures like gold, and the Nālaṭiyār uses the same pair of verbs (ஒறுக்கும் … பொறுக்கும்) to praise the man who could punish but forbears.
155.source: Nālaṭiyār 65 (ch. 7, 'The Absence of Anger: Meekness'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
155._accuracy_note: Checked against Pope's translation on projectmadurai.org; the OCR typo 'wan' is corrected to 'man'. This is a Tamil Jain text. It is a very close verbal echo of ஒறு/பொறு, but it says nothing about the world treasuring the forbearing.

156.quote_or_event: “Leave off the causes of sin, acquire fame through patience! (A man who acts up to this) will rise to the upper regions after having left this body of clay.”
156.explanation: In the lecture on the four rare requisites of the spiritual life, Mahāvīra's disciples are told directly that patience is how lasting fame is won, and that it carries the soul upward after death.
156.tie_back: Valluvar sets the one-day pleasure of revenge against the fame that lasts as long as the world, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise says that fame comes through patience and its reward outlasts this body.
156.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 3.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
156._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. 'Fame through patience' matches the kural's second half directly, but there is no explicit contrast with the short pleasure of revenge.

157.quote_or_event: “To bear with those that speak contemptuous words; yea, more, to say, ‘Ah, will these sink in the other world to hell, the place of fire, as fruit of their contemptuous words;’ and to grieve, is duty of the perfect man.”
157.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār asks the noble person not only to bear an insult but to grieve over the karmic suffering the insulter is storing up for himself.
157.tie_back: Valluvar says that when others wrong us, we should feel sorry for the suffering their wrong will bring them and not retaliate, and the Nālaṭiyār states the same compassion for the wrongdoer's coming fate almost point for point.
157.source: Nālaṭiyār 58 (ch. 6, 'Renunciation'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
157._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on projectmadurai.org. This is a Tamil Jain text, chosen because it is a near one-to-one match for Mu. Varadarasan's reading of நோநொந்து; a canonical parallel is Mahāvīra's compassion toward those who tormented him.

158.quote_or_event: “When persons not our equals say unfitting things, to bear and to be still is worthy conduct. The world girt by foaming waters regards not a contrary course as praise-worthy, but as discreditable.”
158.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār's chapter on patience says that the fitting answer to insolence is to bear it calmly, and that striking back only brings discredit in the world's eyes.
158.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to overcome the arrogant through our own worth (தகுதி), meaning patience, and the Nālaṭiyār uses the same word: bearing such insults quietly is 'worthy conduct' (தகுதி).
158.source: Nālaṭiyār 72 (ch. 8, 'Patience'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
158._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on projectmadurai.org. This is a Tamil Jain text. The shared key word தகுதி makes it a strong fit, though the Nālaṭiyār speaks of bearing insult from inferiors rather than of 'defeating' the arrogant.

159.quote_or_event: “Ceasing to use the stick (i.e. cruelty) against living beings, abandoning the care of the body, the houseless (Mahâvîra), the Venerable One, endures the thorns of the villages (i.e. the abusive language of the peasants), (being) perfectly enlightened.”
159.explanation: The Ācārāṅga's account of Mahāvīra's wanderings in the rough country of Lāḍha shows the great renunciant meeting abuse with endurance instead of retaliation.
159.tie_back: Valluvar says that those who bear the harsh words of transgressors are as pure as renunciants, and the Ācārāṅga shows the model renunciant himself enduring the 'thorns' of abusive speech.
159.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.8.3.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
159._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, where the passage is labelled Book I, Lecture 8, Lesson 3, verse 7 (Jacobi's text). It is a strong fit, though the logic is reversed: the Kural says the patient are like renunciants, while here the renunciant is the one who is patient.

160.quote_or_event: “A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law.”
160.explanation: The same Uttarādhyayana lecture that begins its list of hardships with hunger calls patience under abuse and violence 'the highest good'.
160.tie_back: Valluvar ranks those who fast below those who endure cruel words, and the Uttarādhyayana, which counts hunger among the hardships a monk must bear, likewise names patience the highest good.
160.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.26 (cf. 2.2–3 on hunger) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
160._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The match is partial: the text calls patience the highest good but does not explicitly rank it above fasting, which Jainism itself regards very highly.
